bib.title: AI IDEs or Autonomous Agents? Measuring the Impact of Coding Agents on Software Development

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "AI IDEs or Autonomous Agents? Measuring the Impact of Coding Agents on Software Development", Shyam Agarwal, Hao He, Bogdan Vasilescu (Carnegie Mellon). MSR '26 (23rd Int'l Conf. on Mining Software Repositories), Rio de Janeiro, April 13-14 2026; arXiv:2601.13597v2 (27 Jan 2026). 5-page short paper.

COVERAGE: 5 of 5 pages; 34357 of 34357 chars read (the text came back in one extraction, references included). No appendices. Figure 2 is a plot, so only its caption and axis text were read, not the plotted values.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Agents raise velocity strongly only when they are the repo's first observable AI tool (agent-first, AF). Repos that already used an AI IDE (IDE-first, IF) see little or short-lived gain.
  number: commits +36.25% AF vs +3.06% IF; lines added +76.59% AF vs -6.34% IF (Table 2; commits and lines significant for AF only)
  setup: Staggered DiD, Borusyak et al. imputation estimator, propensity-matched controls. 401 AF repos matched to 606 controls, 117 IF repos matched to 73 controls. Open-source GitHub repos with >=10 stars and >=10 agentic PRs, AIDev v3 data, monthly panel. Intent-to-treat.
  quote: "AF repos see large average gains (+36.3% commits; +76.6% lines added), whereas IF repos show minimal changes (+3.1%; −6.3%)."
  where: p.3, Section 4 and Table 2
- Quality risk is persistent whatever the prior AI exposure. Static-analysis warnings rise about 18% and cognitive complexity about 39%.
  number: warnings +17.73% AF / +19.00% IF; complexity +34.85% AF / +42.87% IF. Warnings are significant for AF only (p<0.001); the IF warnings estimate is not significant. Complexity is significant in both (AF p<0.001, IF p<0.01).
  setup: As above. Metrics from SonarQube, repo-month level. The 18% and 39% figures are rounded from Table 2.
  quote: "Across both AF and IF repositories, static-analysis warnings rise by about 18% and cognitive complexity by roughly 39% (Table 2)."
  where: p.3, Section 4 (Software Quality) and Table 2
- The AF velocity gain is front-loaded and then persists at a lower level. The IF bump is short-lived and later turns negative.
  number: AF at t=0 about +111% commits and +216% lines added; lines added stay +49 to +109% through t=6. IF commits +16 to 28% at t=0-2, then about -35% commits and -61% lines by t=6.
  setup: Event-study dynamic estimates, 6 months after adoption (Figure 2). AF obs=15664, IF obs=3572.
  quote: "AF repositories experience a spike at t=0 (about +111% commits; +216% lines added) and persistently elevated activity, with lines added remaining roughly +49–+109% through t=6."
  where: p.3, Section 4
- Complexity accumulates over time.
  number: AF +20.7% at t=0, about +49% by t=5. IF significantly elevated from t=-2, about +15 to +62% through t=6. Warnings: AF about +22 to +31% at t=4-5, IF about +25% at t=4-6.
  setup: Same event-study.
  quote: "AF repos increase +20.7% at t=0 and reach ∼+ 49% by t=5, while IF repositories become significantly elevated as early as t=−2 and remain ∼+ 15–+62% through t=6."
  where: p.3
- Duplication effects are small and inconsistent, so the authors attribute the quality risk to structural complexity, not copy-paste.
  number: duplicate line density +7.92% AF and -0.94% IF, neither significant
  setup: Table 2
  quote: "Duplication effects are small and inconsistent, suggesting quality risks stem from structural complexity rather than copy–paste proliferation."
  where: p.3
- Comment density rises only in IF repos.
  number: +22.30% IF (p<0.001) vs +4.34% AF (not significant); IF above +30% by t=6
  setup: Table 2
  quote: "IF repositories show substantial and sustained increases (about +22% on average and >+ 30% by t=6), whereas AF effects are muted"
  where: p.3
- The authors read the result as "agent-induced complexity debt": complexity and warnings rise even when velocity gains are weak or negative. This is their interpretation, not a tested mechanism.
  number: none
  quote: "indicate agent-induced complexity debt: agents accelerate the introduction of code that raises long-term cognitive and maintenance load."
  where: p.3
- Prescriptions (not tested): complexity-aware review of agent PRs, routine refactoring, comprehensive automated tests, maintainability metrics surfaced in agent planning and prompting, selective or tightly scoped deployment, provenance tracking.
  number: none
  quote: "AI adoption will need to be paired with strong quality safeguards (e.g., complexity-aware review of agent pull requests, routine refactoring, comprehensive automated tests) to prevent accumulating complexity debt."
  where: p.3, Implications
- Cited from other work (not measured here): maintainers merged most Claude Code PRs, and a controlled experiment found limited productivity benefit for experienced developers.
  number: 83.8% of 567 Claude Code PRs merged (Watanabe et al. 2025)
  quote: "maintainers merge the majority of Claude Code pull requests (83.8% of 567) [42], yet controlled experiments with tools such as Cursor find limited productivity benefits for experienced open-source developers [16]"
  where: p.2, Related Work
- Adoption is dated at the first agent-attributed PR. Attribution uses a cascade: branch prefix, PR author login, first-commit author, GitHub bot type, then default human. Claude PRs are also detected from "Generated with Claude Code" or co-author lines. The authors found misclassifications and missing PRs in AIDev. Prior IDE use is detected from config artifacts for Copilot, Cursor and WindSurf in the latest commit.
  number: none
  quote: "we define the agent adoption date as the earliest month containing an agent-attributed PR."
  where: p.2, Section 3.1

LIMITS
- Conceded: some significant pre-treatment coefficients in warnings and complexity. The authors say these are "not pervasive enough to indicate a sustained pre-trend" but call them "concerning" and "a limitation of our quasi-experimental design and the underlying data."
- Conceded: estimates are intent-to-treat of observable adoption. They cannot measure usage intensity or developer-level interaction. Attribution errors likely add noise and attenuate effects toward zero.
- The IF sample is small (117 treated, 73 controls), which probably explains the wide standard errors (for example IF warnings, +19%, not significant). The IF warnings result is therefore weak evidence.
- Repo-level open-source data only, repos with >=10 stars, adoption mostly April to July 2025 (Figure 1 text says May-July in the caption, April-June in the body). Findings are tied to that tool generation and may have dated.
- AF versus IF is not randomized. The two groups differ (Table 1: IF repos are more starred, forked, and PR-active; AF repos are older but smaller). The "diminishing returns" and "coordination and review overhead" explanations are speculation, not tested.
- The paper does not examine harness, prompt, or agent-configuration differences. It treats "agent" as a bundle across about 12 tools.
- Only one horizon of 6 months is shown. Authors call for longer-horizon work.

BUILDS ON: Borusyak, Jaravel and Spiess 2021 (imputation DiD estimator); He, Miller, Agarwal, Kastner, Vasilescu 2026, "Speed at the Cost of Quality: How Cursor AI Increases Short-Term Velocity and Long-Term Complexity" (design, matching and outcomes replicated and extended); Li, Zhang, Hassan 2025 (AIDev dataset); Becker et al. 2025 (METR experienced-developer RCT); Watanabe et al. 2025 (agentic PRs on GitHub); GHArchive; SonarQube.

CODE: none.

FIGURES
- Figure 1 (p.2): monthly distribution of agent adoption dates, split AF vs IF. Shows adoption clustered in 2025 and that AF repos are more numerous.
- Figure 2 (p.3): six-month event-study effects for the six outcomes, AF vs IF. Shows the AF velocity spike and the IF fade, plus the persistent complexity and warnings rise. Only the caption was read; the plotted values were not.
- Table 1 (p.2): descriptive statistics of treated repos by prior AI exposure.
- Table 2 (p.2-3): average post-adoption effects, which is the source of the main numbers.

PROBLEMS: None embedded. Extraction is clean, apart from table layout and the Figure 1 and Figure 2 axis text, which is jumbled. Fit to the harness pillar is indirect: this is an empirical effects study of agent adoption, not a harness-design paper. Its relevant points are the case for quality gates (complexity and static-analysis checks) and for scoping agent tasks. I have not judged placement in notes 01, 08 or 10.
